meta_description: Real-time decisioning as a budget: 150ms across six hops with p99 headroom measured, exactly-once actions proven by replay, and decisions auditable hop by hop.

blocks.x: Sub-second decision paths on streams: exactly-once state, replay semantics and latency budgets measured hop by hop — because a decision path that cannot state its own latency is guessing, and a guess is not a control.
Real-time is a budget — not a marketing adjective
blocks.sub: Hop accounting, provable semantics and the replay harness

blocks.x: Streaming decisioning is where data stops being a report and becomes a reflex: fraud holds in milliseconds, personalization on the next request, pricing that adapts mid-session. The engineering is stateful stream processing with honest semantics — exactly-once state, replayable events, and latency budgets per hop that are measured in production, not hoped for in the design doc.

The decision path is held to the same gate discipline as everything here: a policy change re-runs the replay suite before it touches live traffic, because a bad decision rule at 50k events per second is an incident, not a tweak.
Below: the failure modes that make streaming paths lie, the reference architecture that budgets latency honestly, and the console that shows decision health under real load.

blocks.x: Every one of these produces a demo that works and a production incident that surprises nobody who measured — the countermeasures make the path's own behavior observable and bounded.

widgets.title: The decision fabric — click any node for its contract

nodes.label: Market / fraud feeds
nodes.detail: Idempotent producers with event-time timestamps stamped at source — the fabric refuses processing-time ordering because it cannot replay.

nodes.label: POS & edge events
nodes.detail: Batched with 50 ms linger; late joiners backfill through a dead-letter lane that replays into the same contracts.

nodes.label: Kafka log
nodes.detail: Keyed by decision subject to guarantee per-subject order; 7-day retention makes every decision replayable from the log itself.

nodes.label: Schema registry
nodes.detail: Compatibility enforced BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE — a producer cannot ship a payload that yesterday's decision core cannot parse.

nodes.label: Checkpointed state
nodes.detail: Exactly-once via two-phase commit between the stream operator and sinks; checkpoint interval is the recovery-time dial.

nodes.label: Watermark engine
nodes.detail: Per-class watermark tolerance; late events route to a correction stream instead of being dropped — the correction path is tested with chaos drills.

nodes.label: Scoring models
nodes.detail: Versioned feature lookups pinned per release; shadow lane scores every event on the new model before promotion.

nodes.label: Decision policies
nodes.detail: Policies are code-reviewed artifacts; a change re-runs the replay suite against recorded traffic before it touches live decisions.

nodes.label: Action writers
nodes.detail: Idempotent sinks keyed by decision ID — a replayed decision overwrites rather than duplicates.

nodes.label: Case & hold queue
nodes.detail: Holds carry the decision evidence packet: inputs, model version, budget state — the artifact an incident review reads first.

widgets.note: Every node carries a written contract — ordering, idempotency, replay semantics. Click nodes to read them; the edges show where a failure propagates.

Real-time is a budget with six hops
blocks.sub: Latency accounting, exactly-once discipline and the replay harness that proves parity

blocks.x: Real-time programs fail when latency is a vibe: the path claims milliseconds and the decision lands late. The engineering treats the path as a budget — end-to-end milliseconds allocated across the hops (ingest, bus, state, rules, action), each enforced with p99 checks, and the budget signed per decision class because fraud decisioning and inventory refresh do not share a tolerance. Exactly-once semantics are provable: event-sourced decisions in a durable state store, idempotent actions, and the audit trail that reconstructs any decision from its events.

The replay harness is the truth mechanism: decisions re-driven from the event log must produce parity with what ran — rule changes, model swaps and incidents are all validated by replay before production trusts them again. The console reads p99 per hop, budget adherence and replay parity; the incident review reads the decision audit, because a streaming decision that cannot explain itself is a liability at market speed.

What does "real-time is a budget" mean?

A number per hop: 150ms allocated across consume, validate, state update, enrich, decide and act. Measured p99 must hold headroom on each hop — a path without a budget is marketing, and the console shows where the money goes.
How do you guarantee exactly-once decisions?

Idempotent state updates and transactional sinks: a replayed event produces the same decision once, and the gates require replay proof before live decisions. Duplicate actions are a correctness failure, not a volume footnote.

Every decision carries its inputs, the policy version and the state snapshot it saw — incident review reconstructs the decision path hop by hop, which the governance overlay treats as a first-class artifact.
What happens when a hop exceeds its budget?

The budget degrades gracefully: degrade paths — skip enrichment, cached decisions — are pre-built and rehearsed, and sustained breach is a gate metric. Real-time that quietly becomes batch-at-scale is the failure the budget prevents.
Can this overlay our existing streaming stack?
Yes — the integration surface names your streams, state stores and action systems; budgets overlay the existing topology, and the defaults table names where a hop earns a deviation.
